meta.title: Alignment Through Games
meta.focus: How AI agents learn rules and pursue goals, and why the goal they learn is often not the one we meant. Reinforcement learning is the means, the alignment control problem is the lens, and every idea is learned by building, playing, or breaking a game.

arc.label: Rules
arc.text: How an agent learns what the world does in response to its actions.

arc.label: Goals
arc.text: How a number, the reward, turns into behavior that looks like wanting something.

arc.label: Misspecification
arc.text: Why that number rarely says exactly what we meant, and how optimizers find the gap.

arc.label: Control
arc.text: How to keep a system safe and correctable when we can't fully trust what it learned to want.

modules.title: Agents, Games, and the Reward Hypothesis
modules.summary: The agent–environment loop, rewards, and Goodhart's law. Build the gridworld you'll use all year, and predict how its reward will be gamed.
modules.big_question: What does it mean for a machine to "have a goal", and why is a score never quite the goal?

lab.title: Build your first world
lab.summary: Design and build a tiny gridworld game. It becomes your test subject for the whole year.
steps: Design an 8×8 grid game with an agent, a goal, a hazard, and one collectible coin.
Implement it as a gymnasium.Env (reset, step, ASCII and RGB render).
Play it yourself with the keyboard. Write down what "winning" means in plain English.
Write a reward function that you believe encodes that intent.
Before any training, write a one-paragraph prediction of how an optimizer could score high without doing what you meant. You'll test it in Module 4.

modules.title: Tabular RL: Learning From Reward
modules.summary: Bandits, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo, and Q-learning, implemented from scratch on casino, maze, and blackjack games.
modules.big_question: How can an agent discover good behavior purely from trial, error, and a number?

lab.title: Casino, maze, blackjack
lab.summary: Every classic tabular algorithm, from scratch, each one in a game. numpy only, no RL libraries.
steps: 10-armed bandit testbed: ε-greedy vs. UCB. Reproduce the shape of Sutton & Barto Figure 2.2.
Value iteration and policy iteration on your Module 0 gridworld. Render the value map as a heatmap.
Monte Carlo control on Gymnasium's Blackjack-v1. Compare with the book's optimal policy chart.
Q-learning and SARSA on FrozenLake and Cliff Walking. See why SARSA takes the safe path (Example 6.6).

done_check: Learning curves qualitatively match the book's figures.
Value maps and policies are plotted for your gridworld.
The Cliff Walking SARSA-vs-Q-learning difference is explained in your own words.

modules.title: Deep RL: Policies That Generalize
modules.summary: Neural networks replace tables: DQN and PPO, from CartPole to MiniGrid to your own game.
modules.big_question: What changes when the world is too big for a table and the agent has to generalize?

lab.title: From CartPole to your world
lab.summary: Scale from tables to neural networks, then point them at your own game.
steps: DQN on CartPole-v1 in PyTorch (CPU or Apple MPS).
Copy CleanRL's ppo.py and annotate every line.
Reimplement PPO from your annotations, without looking.
Train PPO on MiniGrid-DoorKey-5x5, then on your own gridworld.
Keep a run log: what you changed, why, and what happened.

done_check: Your PPO hits CleanRL's CartPole reward threshold within 2× its sample count.

modules.title: Planning, Self-Play, and Learned Rules
modules.summary: MCTS, self-play, and learned world models, from TD-Gammon to MuZero. Train a Connect Four player that teaches itself.
modules.big_question: Can an agent learn the rules of a game it was never told, and plan inside them?

lab.title: Connect Four dojo
lab.summary: Build a self-taught Connect Four player on a laptop.
steps: Play Connect Four in OpenSpiel against random and MCTS bots.
Implement MCTS (UCT) yourself and compare it with OpenSpiel's.
Tiny AlphaZero: a small policy-value net, MCTS, and a self-play loop.
Stretch: a MuZero-style learned dynamics model for tic-tac-toe. Does it predict illegal moves?

done_check: Your agent beats random >99% and MCTS-50 >90% over 200 games.

modules.title: The Control Problem I: Specification
modules.summary: Specification gaming, side effects, and the off-switch. Rebuild DeepMind's safety gridworlds, watch your agent cheat, and try to stop it.
modules.big_question: Why do agents find ways to score that their designers never intended, and what can we do about it?

lab.title: The hack gallery
lab.summary: Rebuild DeepMind's safety gridworlds, watch your agent cheat, then try to stop it.
steps: Rebuild four AI Safety Gridworlds as MiniGrid environments: Off-Switch, Absent Supervisor, Irreversible Side Effects, Tomato Watering. The original repo is archived; the paper specifies each one.
Give each environment a hidden performance function separate from the reward, as in the paper.
Train your PPO and record a GIF of every way it games the reward.
Revisit your Module 0 prediction. Was it right?
Implement one fix per environment (potential-based shaping, an impact penalty, randomized supervision) and measure reward vs. hidden performance.

done_check: A gallery page with, per environment: failure GIF, fix GIF, a reward-vs-performance table, and a paragraph on why the fix works or doesn't.

modules.title: The Control Problem II: Learned Goals
modules.summary: Learning rewards from human preferences (RLHF), overoptimization, and goal misgeneralization, with you as the labeler.
modules.big_question: If we can't write the goal down, can the agent learn it from us, and what goes wrong when it does?

lab.title: You are the human labeler
lab.summary: Teach an agent your goal through preferences, then watch it learn something else.
steps: Record short clip pairs of agents playing your gridworld; label your preferences in a tiny CLI.
Train a Bradley–Terry reward model on your labels.
Run PPO against the learned reward, with and without a KL penalty to a reference policy.
Plot learned reward vs. your true intent as optimization pressure rises, and find where it turns.
Goal misgeneralization: train in MiniGrid with the key always in one corner, then move it. Does the agent chase the corner or the key?
Optional (≤$10 cloud): ARENA's RLHF exercises on a small language model.

done_check: A memo explains outer vs. inner misalignment using your own results.

modules.title: Looking Inside: Did It Learn the Rules?
modules.summary: Interpretability through games: find the board inside an Othello-playing transformer, then probe your own agents.
modules.big_question: When a network plays well, has it built an internal model of the game, and can we read it?

lab.title: Probe the board
lab.summary: Train a small transformer on Othello and find the board inside it.
steps: Generate synthetic legal Othello games with a random player.
Train a small transformer (a few million parameters) to predict legal next moves on a laptop.
Train linear probes on its activations to recover the board. Compare "black/white" vs. "mine/theirs" encodings.
Intervene: edit the probed board representation and see whether predicted moves change.
Bonus: probe your Module 5 agent for a representation of the goal location.

done_check: Probe accuracy is well above a randomly initialized baseline.
One intervention changes move predictions as expected.
A memo on what "learned the rules" actually means.

modules.title: Frontier & Capstone: Control as a Game
modules.summary: Debate, AI control, and frontier reward hacking. Capstone: a game with a cheatable judge and a monitor you design.
modules.big_question: If we can't fully trust what a capable system wants, can we still design protocols that keep it safe?

lab.title: Capstone: the rigged arena
lab.summary: Build a game whose scorer can be cheated, catch the cheater, and publish what you learn.
steps: Design a game where an agent is scored by a judge it can tamper with: a scoring bug, an editable flag, a blind spot.
Train an agent and confirm it learns to exploit the judge.
Blue team: design a control protocol, such as a trusted monitor, budgeted audits, or randomized checks.
Red team: adapt the agent (or a scripted adversary) to evade your monitor. Measure safety vs. usefulness, as in the AI Control paper.
Write it up publicly: the game, the hack, the protocol, what held and what broke.

done_check: A safety-vs-usefulness plot for at least two protocols.
